terms.grammar: noun phrase, with a genitive: minor pars populī
evidence: Cic. Agr. 2.18: ut minor pars populī vocārētur (Lewis & Short, s.v. pars)
terms.comment: The opposite of major pars, the majority (see most). In Cicero’s example, a law had priests chosen by seventeen of the thirty-five tribes, a minority of the people.

evidence: Cic. Leg. 3.32: paucī enim atque admodum paucī
terms.comment: A small number against the many; in politics often the ruling few.

terms.gloss: a minority of the citizens: an ethnic or religious minority
evidence: M-O s.v. minority (ethnic, religious, etc.), after Perugini
terms.comment: For an ethnic minority Morgan–Owens also gives Egger’s minor dīversae stirpis plēbs.

phrases.latin: quod populus per religiōnem sacerdōtia mandāre nōn poterat, ut minor pars populī vocārētur
phrases.english: since religion forbade the people to give priesthoods, (he proposed) that a minority of the people be called to vote

phrases.latin: paucī enim atque admodum paucī honōre et glōriā amplificātī vel corrumpere mōrēs cīvitātis vel corrigere possunt
phrases.english: for a few, a very few, raised high by office and fame, can either corrupt a people’s ways or reform them

sources: Lewis & Short: pars · Lewis & Short: minor · Lewis & Short: paucus
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. minority (ethnic, religious, etc.).
Cicero, De lege agraria 2.18 and De legibus 3.32, checked against the Latin Library texts (CLTK mirror) (11 November 2026).
